questions.stem: Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is

options.text: directly proportional to its absolute temperature

questions.explanation: Boyle's law says that pressure multiplied by volume is constant for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, so if one doubles the other halves. Squeezing the gas into a smaller space makes the molecules strike each unit of wall area more frequently, raising the pressure.

distractorRationale.a: Direct proportionality would mean the gas expands when compressed, which is impossible
distractorRationale.c: That is Charles' law, which applies at constant pressure
distractorRationale.d: Gases are highly compressible, so volume depends strongly on pressure

questions.stem: A gas occupies 500 cm3 at a pressure of 2 atmospheres. At constant temperature, what volume will it occupy at 4 atmospheres?
questions.explanation: Applying P1V1 = P2V2 gives V2 = (2 x 500) / 4 = 1000 / 4 = 250 cm3. Doubling the pressure halves the volume, which is the direct consequence of the inverse relationship.

distractorRationale.a: The pressure ratio was applied twice, dividing by 4 twice over
distractorRationale.c: The pressures were multiplied rather than used as a ratio, giving expansion instead of compression
distractorRationale.d: The volume was multiplied by the final pressure instead of dividing

questions.stem: A gas occupies 300 cm3 at 27 degrees Celsius. At constant pressure, what volume will it occupy at 127 degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation: Convert to kelvin first: T1 = 27 + 273 = 300 K and T2 = 127 + 273 = 400 K. Charles' law gives V2 = V1 x T2/T1 = 300 x 400/300 = 400 cm3. Heating a gas at constant pressure must expand it, so an answer above 300 cm3 is expected.

distractorRationale.a: The temperature ratio was inverted after converting to kelvin, and then misapplied
distractorRationale.b: The Celsius values were used directly, giving 300 x 27/127 rounded
distractorRationale.d: The Celsius values were used directly the other way round, giving 300 x 127/27

questions.stem: Standard temperature and pressure, s.t.p., refers to
questions.explanation: Standard conditions are 0 degrees Celsius, which is 273 K, and a pressure of 760 mmHg, equal to 1 atmosphere or 101325 Pa. These are the conditions under which one mole of any gas occupies 22.4 dm3.

distractorRationale.a: 0 K is absolute zero, at which a gas would have no volume at all
distractorRationale.c: 298 K, that is 25 degrees Celsius, defines room temperature and pressure rather than s.t.p.
distractorRationale.d: 273 degrees Celsius is 546 K, twice the standard temperature

questions.stem: A gas occupies 100 cm3 at 273 K and 760 mmHg. What volume will it occupy at 546 K and 380 mmHg?
questions.explanation: Use V2 = V1 x (P1/P2) x (T2/T1) = 100 x (760/380) x (546/273) = 100 x 2 x 2 = 400 cm3. Both changes expand the gas: halving the pressure doubles the volume, and doubling the absolute temperature doubles it again.

distractorRationale.a: The two effects were assumed to cancel, but both act in the same direction here
distractorRationale.b: Only one of the two changes was applied
distractorRationale.d: The pressure ratio was inverted, treating the change as a compression

questions.stem: A gas at 1.0 atmosphere occupies 250 cm3. It is compressed at constant temperature to 100 cm3. Calculate the new pressure in atmospheres.
questions.explanation: By Boyle's law P2 = P1V1 / V2 = (1.0 x 250) / 100 = 2.5 atmospheres. The volume was reduced to two fifths of its original value, so the pressure had to rise by the reciprocal factor of two and a half.

questions.stem: Using kinetic theory, why does the pressure of a fixed volume of gas rise when it is heated?

options.text: The molecules expand and take up more space
The molecules gain kinetic energy, so they strike the walls harder and more frequently
More gas molecules are created by the heat
The forces of attraction between molecules increase

questions.explanation: Heating raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they travel faster. Each impact on the wall delivers more momentum and the impacts occur more often per second. Since pressure is force per unit area, both effects raise the pressure while the volume is held fixed.

distractorRationale.a: Individual molecules do not change size when heated; only their speed changes
distractorRationale.c: Heating cannot create matter, so the number of molecules is constant
distractorRationale.d: Intermolecular attractions in a gas are negligible and would lower rather than raise pressure
